caseName: Grand Prospect Partners, L.P. v. Ross Dress for Less, Inc.
citation: F067327 (Cal. Ct. App., 5th Dist., Jan. 12, 2015) (unpublished/partially published)
court: California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District
keyFacts: Grand Prospect Partners leased retail space in the Porterville Marketplace shopping center to Ross Dress for Less. When anchor tenant Mervyn's closed after bankruptcy, Ross invoked a cotenancy clause to withhold rent and eventually terminated the lease after a 12-month cure period lapsed. The landlord sued for unpaid rent and termination/future-rent damages, arguing the cotenancy and rent-abatement provisions were unconscionable.
outcome: Jury awarded landlord $672,100 in unpaid rent plus roughly $3.1 million in termination damages (about $3.785 million total, plus ~$916,275 in attorney fees). On appeal, the rent-abatement provision was held an unenforceable penalty (no reasonable relationship to anticipated harm), but the termination provision itself was upheld as valid. Judgment was modified to award only the $672,100 in unpaid rent (final modified judgment approximately $1,588,375.97 with costs).
dollarAmountBasis: Unpaid rent withheld by tenant during dispute period under the cotenancy clause; the $3.1M in additional termination damages was rejected on appeal as an unenforceable penalty
notes: Widely cited California case on when a lease remedy provision (cotenancy/rent-abatement, not a classic 'acceleration' clause) is struck down as an unenforceable penalty versus a valid liquidated-damages-style term. Also available at Justia/law.justia.com (case no. F067327) and caselaw.findlaw.com/ca-court-of-appeal/1691835.html.

keyFacts: Cummings Properties leased commercial office space in Woburn, MA to Massachusetts Constable's Office, Inc. (MCO) under a 5-year lease at $1,364.50/month; defendant Hines personally guaranteed MCO's obligations. MCO defaulted a month after signing, and Cummings invoked the lease's accelerated-rent liquidated-damages clause after MCO vacated and a new tenant was eventually secured about a year later.
outcome: Trial court awarded Cummings $68,650.24, the balance of accelerated rent owed after crediting payments already made and rent from the replacement tenant. The Supreme Judicial Court affirmed, holding the guarantor (a sophisticated businessperson) failed to prove the liquidated-damages clause was an unreasonable forecast of damages at lease signing, applying the 'single look' approach to assess reasonableness at contract formation rather than in hindsight.
dollarAmountBasis: Accelerated remaining rent under the lease's liquidated-damages clause, net of tenant's prior payments and credit for re-letting
notes: Reversed a 2022 Massachusetts Appeals Court decision (Cummings Props., LLC v. Hines, No. 21-P-1153) that had found the same clause an unenforceable penalty; the SJC's 2023 reversal is the controlling precedent. Also reported at law.justia.com/cases/massachusetts/supreme-court/2023/sjc-13406.html.

caseName: SVAP III Poway Crossings, LLC v. Fitness International, LLC
citation: D079903 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, Jan. 20, 2023)
court: California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division One
keyFacts: SVAP III Poway Crossings leased retail space at the Poway Shopping Center to Fitness International (a health club/gym) under a 15-year lease (originally 2002) later extended to 2025. When California's COVID-19 orders forced gyms to close, Fitness stopped paying rent for several months, and the landlord sued for unpaid rent and late fees.
outcome: Trial court granted summary judgment for the landlord, finding $520,361.29 in unpaid rent owed as of October 2021; the Court of Appeal affirmed, holding that force majeure, impossibility, impracticability, and frustration-of-purpose defenses did not excuse the tenant's rent obligation because payment of rent (not operation of the gym) was the relevant contractual performance.
dollarAmountBasis: Unpaid base rent and late fees accrued during COVID-19 closure period, per summary judgment record
notes: One of several 2022-2023 California appellate decisions rejecting COVID-19-based defenses to commercial rent obligations. Also reported at law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2023/d079903.html.

caseName: CSRA Columbus OH Fitness Master Lessee, L.L.C. v. Fitness & Sports Clubs, L.L.C.
citation: 2025-Ohio-2645 (5th Dist. Ct. App., Delaware County, July 24, 2025) (Case No. 24 CAE 08 0052)
court: Ohio Court of Appeals, Fifth Appellate District (Delaware County)
keyFacts: CSRA Columbus, as successor landlord, and Fitness & Sports Clubs (F&S), as successor tenant, were parties to a 20-year lease (through Dec. 2027) for a health/fitness club in Powell, Ohio, with Fitness International as guarantor. In March 2023 F&S sent a notice of surrender, unilaterally vacating years early and telling the landlord it now had 'an obligation to mitigate.' The landlord instead declared default and invoked the lease's accelerated-rent clause, which expressly stated the landlord 'shall not be obligated to relet ... and may recover damages hereunder without such consideration.'
outcome: Trial court granted summary judgment to the landlord and, after a damages hearing, awarded $6,616,025.53 total, including $4,603,463.36 in accelerated rent for the remaining ~3.5 years of the lease term. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that two sophisticated commercial parties may contractually waive the landlord's common-law duty to mitigate, and the express no-mitigation/acceleration language was clear, unambiguous, and enforceable (not a void penalty), even though the landlord in fact tried but failed to re-let the space for 21 months.
dollarAmountBasis: Accelerated base and additional rent for the balance of the 20-year lease term (through Dec. 2027) under an express liquidated-damages/no-mitigation clause, plus other lease charges; $4,603,463.36 of the total specifically represents ~3.5 years of accelerated rent
notes: Full opinion read directly (primary source). Court relied on its own prior precedent, Scott Holding Co. v. Turbo Restaurants US, LLC, 2024-Ohio-5240, and the Ohio Supreme Court's Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone, Inc., 2003-Ohio-3648, which allows landlords and tenants to contract around the default duty to mitigate.

caseName: CPUS Anson Building 8A, LP v. Tradewinds Holding Company, Inc.
citation: Court of Appeals of Indiana (2026) (exact docket number not independently confirmed)
keyFacts: CPUS Anson Building 8A, LP leased industrial warehouse space in Whitestown, Indiana to Tradewinds Holding Company under a lease running February 2021 through February 2026, with monthly base rent plus additional rent for taxes/operating costs. Tradewinds stopped paying rent in April 2022; Anson sued in August 2023, and a replacement tenant (Rockwell) eventually took possession and began paying rent in February 2024.
outcome: After a damages hearing, the trial court awarded Anson $3,559,407.17 plus post-judgment interest, attorney fees, and costs. The Court of Appeals affirmed the finding of breach but reversed and remanded the damages calculation, holding the trial court improperly accrued interest and late fees on the full unpaid balance before subtracting the replacement tenant's rent, instead of crediting the mitigation offset starting when the new tenant's rent obligation began (February 2024).
dollarAmountBasis: Accrued unpaid rent, additional rent, late fees and interest for the remaining lease term, offset by anticipated re-letting income; exact final figure was sent back to the trial court for recalculation
notes: Relied on secondary reporting (Mortgage Professional America) and search-engine summaries rather than a directly retrieved primary opinion; the $3,559,407.17 figure is the trial court's original (since-vacated) award, not a final affirmed number. Treat this figure as illustrative of exposure magnitude in an industrial lease default, not a final judgment amount.

caseName: Bistro Manila, LLC v. Alvah I, LLC
keyFacts: Bistro Manila LLC signed a commercial lease and guaranty in September 2020 to operate a restaurant in a unit of Alvah I/Alvah II's shopping center, with the lease running through July 2028. After Bistro Manila defaulted, the landlord invoked the lease's rent-acceleration clause and argued it had no duty to mitigate. Bistro Manila challenged both the no-mitigation ruling and the enforceability of the acceleration clause as an unenforceable penalty.
outcome: The circuit court entered judgment for the landlord of $410,391.77 in damages plus $18,000 in attorney fees; the Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed, holding the accelerated-rent liquidated-damages clause enforceable (since it included mechanisms preventing over-recovery) and that the landlord had no duty to mitigate under the lease's terms.
dollarAmountBasis: Accelerated remaining rent for the restaurant lease term through 2028, per the lease's liquidated-damages/acceleration clause
notes: Recent (2025) published Virginia appellate decision validating rent-acceleration clauses in commercial restaurant leases; relied on search-derived summaries of the Justia case page rather than a full read of the opinion text.

caseName: Austin Hill Country Realty, Inc. v. Palisades Plaza, Inc.
citation: 948 S.W.2d 293 (Tex. 1997); jury verdict from underlying case at 938 S.W.2d 469 (Tex. App.-Austin 1995)
court: Supreme Court of Texas (jury verdict from Texas Court of Appeals, Third District, Austin)
keyFacts: Palisades Plaza, Inc. leased office space in Austin to Austin Hill Country Realty, a Re/Max real estate brokerage franchise (small business tenant), under a 5-year commercial lease signed September 1992. A dispute over tenant improvements led Palisades to treat the tenants' failure to designate a decision-maker as an anticipatory breach; Palisades sued for breach and future/accelerated rent damages.
outcome: Jury awarded Palisades $29,716 in damages plus $16,500 in attorney's fees; trial court entered judgment on the verdict, and the court of appeals affirmed. The Texas Supreme Court then held, as a matter of first impression for the state, that a commercial landlord has a duty to use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages when a tenant breaches and abandons the lease, unless the lease itself provides otherwise -- rejecting the trial judge's instruction that landlords have no such duty.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury-determined damages for anticipatory breach of a 5-year office lease (remaining/future rent shortfall), plus $16,500 attorney's fees
notes: Leading Texas precedent establishing the commercial landlord's duty to mitigate future/accelerated rent damages; frequently cited as limiting the practical value of acceleration clauses unless mitigation is contractually waived. Underlying jury verdict facts drawn from Justia's summary of the 1995 Texas Court of Appeals decision, 938 S.W.2d 469.

caseName: Fifty States Management Corp. v. Pioneer Auto Parks, Inc.
keyFacts: A commercial lease contained a clause accelerating all remaining rent for the balance of the term upon a single rent default by the tenant, as a condition of the tenant's continued possession (i.e., operative before termination, not just after). The tenant defaulted and challenged the clause as an unenforceable penalty/forfeiture.
outcome: New York's highest court held the acceleration clause enforceable, ruling that where the clause secures the tenant's payment obligations during an ongoing leasehold (rather than being invoked only after the landlord has already terminated the lease and retaken possession), it is generally enforceable absent fraud, exploitative overreaching, or unconscionable conduct; the facts did not warrant equitable intervention.
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed in available secondary sources. Landmark, frequently-cited New York precedent distinguishing acceleration clauses that operate during an ongoing leasehold from those invoked after lease termination/repossession (the latter face more scrutiny). No dollar amount was locatable through search; a full opinion read was not performed.

caseName: Southeastern Land Fund, Inc. v. Real Estate World, Inc.
keyFacts: Foundational Georgia decision (arising from a real estate contract dispute) establishing the state's test for distinguishing an enforceable liquidated-damages provision from an unenforceable penalty, which Georgia courts have since applied to commercial lease rent-acceleration clauses.
outcome: The Georgia Supreme Court held a liquidated-damages provision is enforceable only if: (1) the injury caused by the breach is difficult or impossible to accurately estimate; (2) the parties intended to provide for damages, not a penalty; and (3) the stipulated sum is a reasonable pre-estimate of probable loss. This three-part test became the controlling framework Georgia courts use to evaluate accelerated-rent clauses in commercial leases.
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed. Not itself a commercial lease case on its facts, but it is the controlling Georgia Supreme Court precedent that Peterson v. P.C. Towers and Nobles v. Jiffy Market (below) applied to accelerated-rent clauses.

keyFacts: A commercial landlord sought to enforce an accelerated-rent clause against a defaulting tenant for the full remaining term of the lease. The tenant challenged the clause as an unenforceable penalty under Georgia's Southeastern Land Fund test.
outcome: The Georgia Court of Appeals held the accelerated-rent provision was an unenforceable penalty because it did not calculate damages based on the future rental value of the premises and the likelihood of reletting, meaning it could yield a landlord recovery bearing no reasonable relationship to actual damages.
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed in available sources. This is the case that established Georgia's three-part test (as applied) for accelerated-rent clauses specifically, and is a rare example of a court striking down an acceleration clause for failing to account for re-letting probability/future market rent.

caseName: Nobles v. Jiffy Market Food Store Corp.
keyFacts: Landlord Nobles sought to collect approximately 18 years (nearly 200 monthly payments) of unaccrued future rent at once under an acceleration clause after the tenant, Jiffy Market Food Store, defaulted on a long-term commercial lease.
outcome: The Georgia Court of Appeals held the acceleration clause was an unenforceable penalty, reasoning it contained no mechanism to account for future market conditions, the likelihood of reletting, or resulting rental value, and that awarding the landlord both immediate possession and the entire 18 years of future rent was 'manifestly unreasonable and oppressive.'
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed. Useful illustrative outer-bound case: courts are far more likely to strike an acceleration clause as a penalty the longer the remaining lease term being accelerated (here ~18 years) absent an offset mechanism for re-letting.

caseName: 2460-68 Clark, LLC v. Chopo Chicken, LLC
keyFacts: Landlord 2460-68 Clark, LLC leased retail space in Chicago to Chopo Chicken, LLC (a small restaurant business) at $5,650/month rent, with an individual guarantor, under a lease running through August 2021 (twice amended). After tenant default, the landlord pursued eviction and future/liquidated rent damages in a combined forcible-entry-and-detainer and damages action.
outcome: The trial court found in favor of the landlord, awarding possession and monetary damages. The Illinois Appellate Court held that a lease clause providing for 'a sum equal to the amount of unpaid rent and other charges ... for the balance of the term' as damages for tenant default constituted a valid liquidated-damages provision (rather than a simple rent-acceleration clause), which can be recovered without offset for reletting in a combined possession-and-damages action -- offering landlords a way around the practical difficulty of estimating relet credits while the defaulting tenant remains in possession.
notes: Exact damages figure awarded was not confirmed through available secondary sources (monthly rent was $5,650; lease term length for damages calculation not independently verified). Notable for the practical drafting guidance it gives Illinois commercial landlords: structure damages as liquidated damages rather than a bare acceleration clause to avoid Illinois's forcible-entry-and-detainer mitigation complications under 735 ILCS 5/9-213.1.

caseName: Sylva Shops Limited Partnership v. Hibbard
keyFacts: Sylva Shops Limited Partnership leased out-parcel commercial space in a shopping center to a small business, 'The Bagel Bin and Sandwich Shop,' run by tenants Hibbard and Gedney under a 5-year lease beginning April 2002. The tenants closed the shop after only about five months (September 2002) due to declining sales, and the landlord sued for unpaid rent for the remainder of the term.
outcome: At trial, actual damages were calculated at $35,511.70, but the jury applied a mitigation offset of $22,401.70, awarding the landlord only $13,110.00. On appeal, the North Carolina Court of Appeals held the lease's clause relieving the landlord of any duty to mitigate was enforceable and not against public policy, vacating the reduced verdict and remanding for entry of judgment on the full $35,511.70 in actual damages without any mitigation offset.
dollarAmountBasis: Unpaid and future rent for the remainder of a 5-year lease term after a small-business tenant (bagel shop) closed 5 months into the lease, with no mitigation offset because the lease validly waived the landlord's duty to mitigate
notes: Good illustrative small-business/retail fact pattern with a modest dollar figure. Initial jury verdict was $13,110 (net of an improperly-applied mitigation offset); the correct, appellate-endorsed recovery figure is the full $35,511.70. Relied on a findlaw case-summary extraction rather than the full opinion text.

keyFacts: Foundational Colorado decision addressing a commercial landlord's remedies and obligations after a tenant abandons leased premises mid-term, including the landlord's ability to seek damages for the remaining term of the lease.
outcome: The Colorado Supreme Court held that a commercial landlord seeking damages for a tenant's abandonment of the leasehold (including future/remaining-term rent) owes a duty to take commercially reasonable steps to mitigate those damages by attempting to re-let the premises; a landlord's recovery of remaining-term rent will be reduced by amounts it did or should have recovered through reasonable re-letting efforts.
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed in available sources. Colorado's foundational mitigation-duty precedent for commercial lease future-rent damages, analogous to Texas's Austin Hill Country Realty and Ohio's Frenchtown Square.

caseName: Tempe Corporate Office Building v. Arizona Funding Services, Inc.
keyFacts: A commercial office landlord sought to enforce a lease clause allowing recovery of future/remaining-term rentals after a tenant default, in a dispute over the scope of the landlord's remedies and mitigation obligations under Arizona law.
outcome: The Arizona Court of Appeals upheld the lease clause providing for recovery of future rentals, holding that a commercial landlord may sue for all unpaid rent and other sums due under the lease, provided the landlord satisfies its duty to mitigate damages by making reasonable efforts to re-let the premises.
notes: Principle only, no dollar figure disclosed in available sources. Cited as Arizona's leading case confirming enforceability of future-rent recovery clauses conditioned on the landlord's mitigation efforts (see also Wingate v. Gin, 148 Ariz. 289 (App. 1985), and Lee Dev. Co. v. Papp, 166 Ariz. 471 (App. 1990)).

caseName: Copinol Restaurant, Inc. v. 26 North Market LLC
keyFacts: Copinol Restaurant, Inc. leased commercial space in Frederick, Maryland from 26 North Market LLC under a lease running through March 2032. Copinol missed a $13,917 rent payment due in May 2023, and the landlord terminated the lease and pursued eviction/possession under Maryland's tenant-holding-over statute (Real Property § 8-402).
outcome: The District Court of Maryland initially granted possession to the landlord; on appeal, Maryland's Supreme Court held that the tenant-holding-over statute applies only where a lease has expired by lapse of its own term, not where a landlord has terminated the lease early for a rent default -- meaning the landlord could not use that summary statutory remedy for an early termination based on unpaid rent, even though the underlying nonpayment was undisputed.
notes: Principle only for damages purposes -- the case turned on which eviction procedure applies after a rent default, not on a monetary judgment amount, though the underlying missed payment was $13,917. Included for jurisdictional diversity and because it illustrates a procedural pitfall (choice of eviction remedy) that affects how landlords actually recover unpaid/future rent in Maryland.
